pages.name: The line
pages.text: This is the line, `y = x`, the first of five graph shapes. Drag the marker and the point rides the line while the table fills in. Inputs 1, 2, 3 give 1, 2, 3, so each equal step across gives the same rise, and doubling the input doubles the output.

pages.text: This is the square, `y = x²`. A negative input gives the same output as the positive one, so −3 and 3 both give 9, and the curve is a U, called a [[parabola]]. Its outputs 0, 1, 4, 9 rise by 1, 3 and 5, and on a 1 Ω cable run 3 A loses 9 W.

pages.name: Double the current
pages.task: A 1 Ω run loses 9 W at 3 A. How much does it lose at 6 A?
pages.why: Double the current and the loss goes up four times, because `2 × 2 = 4`. So 6 A loses `6 × 6 × 1 = 36` W, not the 18 W a line would give.

pages.name: The cube
pages.text: This is the cube, `y = x³`. 1 gives 1 and 2 gives 8, so doubling the input makes the output eight times, and a negative input gives a negative output, so −2 gives −8 and the curve is an S that flattens through 0. A ship's engine load goes with the cube of propeller speed, a model that works well at steady high speed but breaks down at partial load.

pages.task: A fan's power goes with the cube of its speed. What share of full power does it use at half speed?
pages.why: Power goes with the cube of speed, so half speed gives `0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125` of full power, which is 12.5%, one eighth.

pages.name: The one-over
pages.text: This is the one-over, `y = 1/x`. Double the input and the output halves, so on a 12 V supply 3 Ω draws 4 A and 6 Ω draws 2 A. There is no point at 0: from the right the curve runs off up the side, and negative inputs make a second curve that runs off down it.

pages.name: Double the resistance
pages.task: On the 12 V supply, 3 Ω draws 4 A. How much does 6 Ω draw?
pages.why: Double the resistance and the current halves, because 12 shared by twice as much is half as much. `12 ÷ 6 = 2` A.

pages.name: The square root
pages.text: This is the square root, `y = √x`. It starts at 0 with nothing to its left (lesson 4 says why), and its outputs 1, 2, 3 need inputs 1, 4, 9, so it rises steeply, then flattens. As `√0.5 = 0.707`, a flow meter at 50% of its full pressure difference shows 71% of its full flow.

pages.name: A quarter of the difference
pages.task: What flow does 25% of the full pressure difference give?
pages.why: Flow is the square root of the pressure difference, and `0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25`, so a 25% difference gives 50% flow.

pages.name: Which currents
pages.task: Which currents lose 9 W in the 1 Ω run? A negative current is the same current flowing the other way.
pages.why: The level line at 9 W cuts the U at −3 A and at 3 A, because `3 × 3 = 9` and `−3 × −3 = 9`. So 3 A loses 9 W whichever way it flows.
